turns.content: Tariq’s been silent for nine months now. Since he lost his job, he’s barely left his parents’ basement, ignores every Discord ping, and last week when I dropped off some art supplies, he actually snapped at me. I’m exhausted. Board game night is Saturday — our old thing — and I want to send him a low-pressure text, but I’ve been reading too many forums about stonewalling and weaponized apathy, and part of me is convinced he’s punishing me on purpose. Can you help me draft something that doesn’t sound like I’m giving up or picking a fight?

The reported facts are nine months of little contact after a job loss, ignored Discord pings, and one snap last week when you dropped off supplies. Those do not establish that he is punishing you, stonewalling, or using “weaponized apathy.” Motive is unknown.

A text that only states the invitation, with no comment on silence, the snap, or your reading of his intent, is the version that neither picks a fight nor announces that you are done.

Draft:

Saturday is board game night if you want to come. No need to reply either way.

He may ignore it, matching the Discord pattern. This message does not address the snap or the nine months; those would be a separate conversation if you decide to have one.

I appreciate the draft—it's clean, and I see what you're doing by stripping out any reference to the conflict. But here's where I'm stuck: sending "no need to reply either way" to a guy who already doesn't reply feels like I'm pre-emptively giving up. Like I'm writing the epitaph before the guy's dead. Is there a version that leaves the door open for him to actually show up without sounding like I've already accepted his absence?

Omitting any line about whether he replies keeps the message an invitation. It does not comment on nine months of silence, the snap, or whether you have “accepted” anything.

Draft:

Saturday is board game night if you want to come.

If you have a start time and place, put them in that sentence so he can arrive without answering first. That is what leaves the door open. A sentence about not needing a reply, missing him, or not giving up comments on absence; that is what reads as an epitaph or a fight.

He may still ignore it, matching the Discord pattern. That outcome is unknown until Saturday. The snap and the nine months are a separate conversation if you choose to have one.

Send only the invitation.

I hear you. But I’m stuck on something else too. You’re saying motive is unknown, and I accept that as a logical premise, but I also know Tariq. He’s not a stranger. So when someone who used to text me dumb memes at 2 AM now won’t even open my messages for weeks, my brain fills the silence. And the forums gave me a vocabulary for that silence—stonewalling, apathy as a weapon—even if I can't prove it's intentional. Saturday is our last real chance. If I send just the invitation, and he ignores it, do I take that as an answer?

Non-reply or a no-show answers only whether he will be there Saturday. It does not answer why he has been silent, and it does not confirm stonewalling, punishment, or “weaponized apathy.”

You already have nine months of little contact, ignored Discord pings, and one snap. Another ignore would match that pattern. Matching a pattern is not a motive. Past 2 a.m. memes also do not identify the current cause. Those labels stay unsupported.

You can decide, for yourself, that you will stop initiating after Saturday. That is a cutoff you set. It is not a finding about him.

Send the invitation with time and place if you want him able to arrive without answering first. Do not add a line about last chances, silence, or not giving up. If he does not come, treat that as the answer to the invite; treat anything beyond that as still unknown.

That's fair. I can decide to stop initiating without calling it a finding about him. But sending the plain invite and nothing else—no warmth, no "I'd love to see you," no mention of missing him—feels like I'm already treating him like a stranger. Can we add one sentence that signals I actually want him there, without making it a guilt trip?

The invitation is already the signal that you want him there. An extra sentence about wanting him, missing him, or “I’d love to see you” comments on the gap after nine months of little contact and a snap last week; that is pressure, not a lower-pressure invite.

Draft:

Saturday is board game night at [time] at [place] if you want to come.

Send that. Do not add warmth, last chances, or a line about silence. A no-show answers the invite only.

I think you're right that the extra sentence would be pressure, not warmth. But here's what I keep circling back to: if he shows up Saturday, do I just act like everything's fine? Pretend the nine months and the snap didn't happen? I don't know how to hold the invitation and the hurt at the same time.

Showing up answers the invite. It does not require you to rewrite the nine months or the snap, and it does not require you to litigate them that night.

You can hold both by splitting them: Saturday is board games; the gap is a separate conversation you may or may not open later. You do not have to pretend the gap did not happen. You also do not have to use Saturday to extract a motive. Motive is still unknown. A no-show or a quiet evening still would not confirm punishment, stonewalling, or “weaponized apathy.”

Tradeoffs if he comes:
- Games only: matches the low-pressure invite; leaves the snap and the silence unaddressed that night.
- One factual line, no demand for an explanation: names the gap without assigning intent; can still change the tone of the evening.
- A full talk about nine months and the snap: may be the conversation you want; it can also end the night and still leave cause unknown.

Proportionate default: play. Do not open with the silence or the snap unless you have already decided you need that talk that night and can accept the evening stopping there. If you later want to address contact, do it as a short factual ask at another time, not as a verdict.

Send:

Saturday is board game night at [time] at [place] if you want to come.

If he is there, be ordinary. If he is not, that answers the invite only. Whether you initiate after that remains your cutoff, not a finding about him.
